topic: How do young people use AI for school and work, and what do they believe about it?
intro: AI chatbots arrived in classrooms fast, and surveys now show how students actually use them. Most young people have tried AI, but far fewer rely on it for most of their work, and their mood is cooling: excitement is down and worry about learning and jobs is up. This page looks at what the numbers say, possible reasons, and how to judge claims about "a whole generation" and AI. Most data is American; one Canadian survey and one Statistics Canada study are included.

data.stat: 45% of US teens aged 13-17 say they do none of their schoolwork with AI chatbots; 10% do most or all of it with them.
data.detail: Pew asked 1,458 teens (Sept 25-Oct 9, 2025; margin ±3.3): 21% said some and 23% a little. 64% have used a chatbot at all. Teens who use AI for school mostly research topics (48%), solve math problems (43%) and edit their own writing (35%). 59% think classmates use AI to cheat at least somewhat often; 15% are not sure.

data.stat: In Gallup's 2026 survey of Americans aged 14-29, 22% felt excited about AI, down 14 points in a year; 31% felt angry, up 9.
data.detail: 1,572 people, Feb 24-Mar 4, 2026 (margin ±3.6), with the Walton Family Foundation and GSV. Curiosity (49%) and anxiety (42%) were the most common feelings. 51% use generative AI at least weekly and 19% never. 80% think AI will make learning harder in future.

data.stat: 73% of Canadian students surveyed use generative AI for schoolwork, up from 52% in 2023; 66% say they are learning and retaining less.
data.detail: KPMG Canada online survey, Aug 15-Sept 15, 2025, of 684 students, mostly in college or university (only 15% of the AI users were in high school). 71% say their grades improved, 57% feel they are cheating when they use it, and 77% want courses on using AI.

data.stat: 59% of Americans aged 18-29 see AI as a threat to their job prospects, more than outsourcing (48%) or immigration (31%).
data.detail: Harvard Youth Poll, 2,040 people, Nov 3-7, 2025 (margin ±2.94). Asked whether AI will create or take away opportunities for them, 44% said take away, 14% create, 17% no change and 23% were unsure.

data.stat: About 10% of Canadian workers aged 15-24 used generative AI at work in the past year, versus 27% of those aged 25-54.
data.detail: Statistics Canada, from four waves of a working-conditions survey (Sept 2024-July 2025). StatCan says the age gap is mostly explained by the kinds of jobs young people hold; after adjusting, the difference was no longer statistically significant.

why.claim: AI saves time, and many students use it for help rather than to do the whole job.
why.detail: Research, math help and editing are the top school uses in Pew's survey.[^1] In Gallup's survey 56% say AI helps them get work done faster, though that is down 10 points from a year earlier.[^2] KPMG found 45% of Canadian students turn to AI first rather than writing their own draft.[^4]

why.claim: Students see better grades in the short term, even when they worry they learn less.
why.detail: 71% of Canadian students in KPMG's survey say AI improved their grades, while 66% say they learn and remember less.[^4] No survey here asked directly whether grade pressure drives AI use, so the link is a reasonable guess, not a measurement.

why.claim: Schools are writing rules that allow some AI use, which makes it normal.
why.detail: 74% of US students in Gallup's survey say their school has AI rules, up from 51%, and 65% of those with a policy are allowed to use AI for schoolwork; only 28% say the school provides AI tools.[^2] That rules are spreading is measured; that they cause more use is not.

why.claim: Worry about entry-level jobs is making young people more negative about AI.
why.detail: The worry itself is measured: 59% of young Americans see AI as a job threat[^5], and 64% of Canadian students fear AI is cutting entry-level roles.[^4] Whether AI is actually removing those jobs is still debated; StatCan finds young workers' lower AI use reflects the jobs they hold.[^6]

why.claim: Many doubt AI is good for thinking and fairness, which may explain the falling excitement.
why.detail: 42% in Gallup's survey say AI harms careful thinking and only 25% say it helps; only 28% trust AI-assisted work.[^2] 41% believe most classmates use AI when they are not supposed to.[^3] These views are measured; that they cause the cooling mood is a judgment.

test: Who was surveyed: high-school students, university students, young workers, or all young adults? Do the results really apply to people your age?
Does the headline number describe trying AI once, using it weekly, or relying on it for most work? These are very different things.
Is a claim that AI is 'taking jobs' backed by data on actual jobs, or only by what people fear will happen?
Who paid for the survey (a tech company, a consultancy, a foundation), and could that shape which questions were asked?
